---
title: "Figure 8: Impact of El Niño on Inflation"
---

![Python: `python/fig-8-0.py`](../images/python/fig-8-0.png)

The estimated cumulative impact of an El Niño event on inflation in two
regions, the Andean countries and CAPDR, over the 12 quarters after the
event. Quarter 0 is the start of the event. Each line is an estimate from a
local projection, and each shaded area its confidence band (10th to 90th
percentile). Where a band lies entirely above zero, the effect is clearly
positive.

**New in this chart:** two bands kept in one dictionary. It is very similar
to [Figure 1.1.2](fig-1-1-2.qmd), and the two pages are worth comparing.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 13 rows (quarters 0 to 12):

| category | Dummy1 | Dummy2 | Dummy3 | Dummy4 | Andean | CAPDR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | -0.01 | 0.67 | -0.86 | 0.92 | 0.33 | 0.26 |

`Dummy1` to `Dummy4` are the stacked-area helper series for the two bands.
In Excel, two bands on one chart are built as one stack of four areas:

| Series | Role | Visible? |
|---|---|---|
| `Dummy1` | from zero to the bottom of the Andean band | no |
| `Dummy2` | the Andean band | yes |
| `Dummy3` | from the top of the Andean band to the bottom of the CAPDR band | no |
| `Dummy4` | the CAPDR band | yes |

`Dummy3` can be negative, as in the first row (-0.86): the CAPDR band then
starts *below* the top of the Andean band, and the two overlap.

`Andean` and `CAPDR` are the estimates, drawn as lines.

## The script

### The band edges

```python
# In Excel, the confidence bands are drawn as stacked areas, built from four
# helper series (Dummy1-Dummy4). Adding them up gives the band edges.
d1, d2, d3, d4 = (data[f"Dummy{i}"] for i in range(1, 5))
bands = {
    "Andean": (d1, d1 + d2, "#D8C8DE"),
    "CAPDR": (d1 + d2 + d3, d1 + d2 + d3 + d4, "#F3C9AD"),
}
line_colours = {"Andean": "#5A2875", "CAPDR": "#C95716"}
```

The first line reads the four helper columns in one go:

- `f"Dummy{i}"` is an *f-string*: the `{i}` is replaced by the value of
  `i`, so it gives `"Dummy1"`, `"Dummy2"`, and so on.
- `(... for i in range(1, 5))` produces the four columns one after another,
  for i = 1, 2, 3, 4.
- `d1, d2, d3, d4 = ...` assigns them to four names, in order.

It is a compact version of four lines: `d1 = data["Dummy1"]`, and so on.

The band edges are running totals of the helper series, as explained in
[Shaded bands](../techniques.qmd#sec-bands):

- **Andean band**: from `d1` to `d1 + d2`.
- **CAPDR band**: stacked on top of the Andean band, after the invisible gap
  `d3`, so from `d1 + d2 + d3` to `d1 + d2 + d3 + d4`.

Each band is stored with its colour as a triple (lower, upper, colour). The
band colours are pale versions of the line colours: light purple for the
Andean band, light orange for CAPDR.

### The frame

`new_chart()` is called with `bottom_gap=0.5`, because there is an axis
title ("Quarters") under the quarter numbers.

### The bands

```python
for lower, upper, colour in bands.values():
    ax.fill_between(quarters, lower, upper, color=colour, alpha=0.55, linewidth=0)
```

`.values()` loops over the triples only, without the names, and unpacks each
one into `lower`, `upper` and `colour`. The names in `bands` are not used by
the script; they are there so the dictionary is easy to read.

`alpha=0.55` makes the bands about half transparent, so where they overlap
both colours show, and the overlap appears as a mix of the two. Without
transparency, the CAPDR band, drawn second, would hide the Andean band where
they overlap. The colours are chosen light enough that, even half
transparent, they stay in the background.

### The axis line and the lines

```python
# The x-axis is drawn at zero, with short tick marks pointing down; the
# quarter labels stay at the bottom of the chart.
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.vlines(quarters, -0.08, 0, color="black", linewidth=0.6)

for series, colour in line_colours.items():
    ax.plot(quarters, data[series], color=colour, linewidth=2.0,
            solid_capstyle="round", label=series)
```

- **An axis line at zero**, drawn over the bands, with short ticks pointing
  down from 0 to -0.08 at each quarter, as in the published chart. See [An axis line
  at zero](../techniques.qmd#sec-axis-line).
- **The two lines**, drawn last, so they lie on top of the bands and the
  axis line. They are 2 points wide, in the full-strength colours.

Only the lines have a `label`, so the legend shows the two regions as lines,
not the bands. The caption explains the shaded areas.

### The axes and the legend

```python
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 12.5)
ax.set_xticks(quarters)
ax.set_xlabel("Quarters", fontsize=9, labelpad=7)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, -2, 5, 1)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2.3)

ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.05, 0.98), handlelength=3.0,
          labelspacing=0.4)
```

- **The x-axis** runs half a quarter beyond 0 and 12, and every quarter is
  labelled. The quarters are numbers, so they go on the axis directly.
- **The axis title** "Quarters" is written with `ax.set_xlabel()`, 7 points
  below the numbers.
- **The bottom spine** and its ticks are hidden, because the axis line is at
  zero.
- **The y-axis** runs from -2 to 5 with a tick every 1, so zero is a tick.
- **The legend** sits in the top left, with a little more space between the
  two entries than usual (`labelspacing=0.4`).

## Comparing with Figure 1.1.2

[Figure 1.1.2](fig-1-1-2.qmd) also has two confidence bands built from the
same four kinds of Excel helper series. Its script stores each band's edges
in a variable of its own (`blue_band`, `orange_band`) and draws the bands
with two separate `fill_between()` calls, each with its own settings. This
one keeps each band's edges and colour together in a dictionary and draws
all bands in one loop. The second approach is easier to extend: a third band would be one
more entry in `bands`.

## Changing the chart

- **Opaque bands.** If the bands do not overlap in a new edition, drop
  `alpha=0.55` and use slightly lighter colours.
- **Bands in the legend.** Give each band a `label`, for example by storing
  a fourth item in each triple, and pass it to `fill_between()`.
- **A third region.** Add its band (two more helper columns) and its line
  colour; the loops need no change.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-8-0.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-8-0.py"}
"""Figure 8: Impact of El Niño on Inflation."""
from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart, set_y_scale

STEM = "fig-8-0"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)
quarters = data["category"]

# In Excel, the confidence bands are drawn as stacked areas, built from four
# helper series (Dummy1-Dummy4). Adding them up gives the band edges.
d1, d2, d3, d4 = (data[f"Dummy{i}"] for i in range(1, 5))
bands = {
    "Andean": (d1, d1 + d2, "#D8C8DE"),
    "CAPDR": (d1 + d2 + d3, d1 + d2 + d3 + d4, "#F3C9AD"),
}
line_colours = {"Andean": "#5A2875", "CAPDR": "#C95716"}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Impact of El Niño on Inflation",
    subtitle="(Percent; cumulative impact)",
    caption=(
        "Source: IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: Shows the estimated impact of El Niño events on inflation using the\n"
        "local projection method in a cross-country panel. Shaded areas\n"
        "correspond to 10th/90th percentile confidence intervals. Andean =\n"
        "Colombia, Ecuador, Peru; CAPDR = Central America, Panama, and the\n"
        "Dominican Republic."
    ),
    left=0.3,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.5,
)

for lower, upper, colour in bands.values():
    ax.fill_between(quarters, lower, upper, color=colour, alpha=0.55, linewidth=0)

# The x-axis is drawn at zero, with short tick marks pointing down; the
# quarter labels stay at the bottom of the chart.
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.vlines(quarters, -0.08, 0, color="black", linewidth=0.6)

for series, colour in line_colours.items():
    ax.plot(quarters, data[series], color=colour, linewidth=2.0,
            solid_capstyle="round", label=series)

ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 12.5)
ax.set_xticks(quarters)
ax.set_xlabel("Quarters", fontsize=9, labelpad=7)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=0, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, -2, 5, 1)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", direction="in", length=2.3)

ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.05, 0.98), handlelength=3.0,
          labelspacing=0.4)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
